{'name': 'knowledge/handbook-case.md', 'section': {'number': '3', 'title': '3. Time and demand series', 'start': 15682, 'size': 2769}, 'start': 0, 'total': 2769, 'text': '# 3. Time and demand series

## 3.1 Power and energy

A demand series gives **power** per step (`MW`). A daily file usually gives the mean power of
the day; a column in `MWh/d` is an energy, not a power, and is a unit to confirm. `MWth`,
`MWcool`, `MWc` are all `MW`: the suffix names the product. `MWe` is electricity, another
product. A demand derived from gas bills is fuel burnt, not heat delivered: ask which a file
holds.

## 3.2 The time axis and the time zone

- `time.start` and `time.end` without an offset are UTC; `end` is excluded
  (`gemini/gemini/case/time.py`).
- A **series** needs an offset (`2027-01-01T00:00:00Z`) on every timestamp, or a `time_zone`
  (an IANA name such as `Europe/Amsterdam`) for the file. Without both, gemini refuses the
  series: there is no default zone (`gemini/gemini/units/inputs.py`, `from_series`).
- With a `time_zone` and a step of one day or more, gemini matches the rows to the case's steps
  by local calendar date, so a 23- or 25-hour day of daylight saving does no harm.
- A zone that no file and no user message states is an assumption: propose it in the one
  question with its reason (the site's location), `source: agent`, never "the user chose it".
- The time column is read as `time`; a column of another name (`date`) is named in `columns`
  when the file is given (skill `setting-the-case`).
- A year has 365 or 366 daily rows; check against the calendar.
- The economic analysis period (often decades) is an economics value, not `time`.

## 3.3 Checks on a demand series

Report each failure as a flaw (§1.4); correct none.

| Check | Fails when |
|---|---|
| count | rows differ from the span over the step |
| gaps, duplicates | a missing or repeated time |
| sign, finite | a negative or non-finite value (gemini refuses them) |
| unit | the peak or total is far from the brief's values for checking (§1.3) |
| season | heating peaks in summer or cooling in winter (northern hemisphere) |
| span | the case's span differs from the file's: the span is wrong, never the data |
| zero days | many zero days of cooling are normal; note how many (they matter for `when`, §6.6) |
| base load | a heating series that never reaches zero has a summer base: say so |

## 3.4 Resolution

| Step | Shows | Hides |
|---|---|---|
| hourly | daily pattern, true peak, storage cycles | nothing relevant for sizing |
| daily | season, cold spells, days a source runs | the hourly peak, which is higher than the daily mean |
| monthly | season only | peaks, cold spells, zero days |

A daily case sizes on daily means: name the hidden hourly peak as a limitation. Never build a
finer series from a coarser one, nor a series from a peak and an annual energy: ask for a
series file, the values, or a constant power.

---

  the 30 MW heating peak needs two or three doublets, or fewer with a heat pump and a boiler.

# 3 The subsurface

This chapter gives the reservoir values a design needs and how they follow from depth: temperature,
pressure, productivity, drawdown, thermal breakthrough. Most of them are properties of the site
(the case) and only the depth and well design are choices.

## 3.1 Reservoir temperature from the gradient

In conductive settings the temperature rises roughly linearly with depth:

T(z) = T_surface + G · z

with T_surface the mean surface (or reference) temperature and G the geothermal gradient. Typical
continental gradients are of the order of 25 to 35 K/km; sedimentary basins with thick insulating
cover can be higher [textbook: Stober and Bucher 2013]. The gradient of a site comes from the case
(measured wells, maps), never from a typical value.

In gemini the plant states only the depth; the case holds `site.ground.gradient` and
`site.ground.surface_temperature`, and the run derives the reservoir temperature at the plant's

matches.text:
- `time.start` and `time.end` without an offset are UTC; `end` is excluded
  (`gemini/gemini/case/time.py`).
- A **series** needs an offset (`2027-01-01T00:00:00Z`) on every timestamp, or a `time_zone`
  (an IANA name such as `Europe/Amsterdam`) for the file. Without both, gemini refuses the
  series: there is no default zone (`gemini/gemini/units/inputs.py`, `from_series`).
- With a `time_zone` and a step of one day or more, gemini matches the rows to the case's steps
  by local calendar date, so a 23- or 25-hour day of daylight saving does no harm.
- A zone that no file and no user message states is an assumption: propose it in the one
  question with its reason (the site's location), `source: agent`, never "the user chose it".
- The time column is read as `time`; a column of another name (`date`) is named in `columns`
  when the file is given (skill `setting-the-case`).
- A year has 365 or 366 daily rows; check against the calendar.
- The economic analysis period (often decades) is an economics value, not `time`.

## 3.3 Checks on a demand series

Report each failure as a flaw (§1.4); correct none.

# 12. Worked example: a brief with daily demand files

A general pattern with **invented numbers** (a fictional town, "Northbay"). It shows the method
of chapters 0 to 11 end to end; no number here is a value for any real case. A competition or a
client case keeps its own values in its own assumptions document in Knowledge (§8.2).

## 12.1 Inputs

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `Northbay_Heat_Daily.csv` | `day`, `heat_MWth`: one row per day of one year, dates without offset |
| `Northbay_Cold_Daily.csv` | `day`, `cold_MWc`: same days |
| `Northbay_Brief.pdf` | 3 pages: supply temperatures, reservoir, brine, rules, freedoms |

Lessons:
- the time column is `day`: name it in `columns` when the files are given (§3.2);
- the dates have no offset: each series needs a `time_zone`. The brief names the site but no
  zone, so the zone is an assumption with its reason (the site's location) in the one question
  (§3.2, §0.3);
- the brief is the only source of rules; read every note under its tables (§1.1).

## 12.2 Values for checking

The brief says (p. 1): "heating peak 18 MW in January, 70 GWh per year; cooling peak 6 MW in
July". These check the CSV files (§1.3): a peak of 18,000 in the file would be kW; a cooling
peak in January a column swap. The case takes the series, never these numbers. gemini's
`read_profile` summary gives the file's own peak and total for the comparison.

## 12.3 Classifying the brief

# 3. Time and demand series

## 3.1 Power and energy

A demand series gives **power** per step (`MW`). A daily file usually gives the mean power of
the day; a column in `MWh/d` is an energy, not a power, and is a unit to confirm. `MWth`,
`MWcool`, `MWc` are all `MW`: the suffix names the product. `MWe` is electricity, another
product. A demand derived from gas bills is fuel burnt, not heat delivered: ask which a file
holds.

## 3.2 The time axis and the time zone

Read, choose, complete, size, simulate a short window, check, fix, simulate the whole period,
optimise, compare (the steps of 0.1). Steps from simulate to fix repeat until the check passes.
When three changes aimed at one failing requirement make no progress, the structure is wrong, not
the numbers: change the family (8.2) or report the conflict (0.1, stop rule; QA-090 in 12.7).

## 1.5 Values, sources and the no-defaults rule

[gemini: `docs/rules.md`, "No defaults"]

- **No default values.** Nothing a user must decide has a default in gemini; a missing value is an
  error that names its path.
- **Every value has a source**: the user's files, Knowledge, a connector, the web, and only then a
  labelled assumption with its reason (0.6; skills `finding-sources`, `connectors`, `web-search`).
- **Derive, never guess**: a number that can be computed is computed with a tool (`calculator`,
  `python`, `evaluate_module`) and cited by its calculation.

The typical values in chapters 2 to 9 orient a first guess and help to recognise a wrong result;
they are inputs only through 0.7 with their label.

hot water or process heat). Read for each:

matches.text:
- **Whether the brine can supply the heat directly.** The brine must be hotter than the supply
  temperature by at least the approach of the exchanger (6.1). If not, a heat pump, a boiler or
  deeper wells must close the gap (6.3).
- **How much heat a kilogram of brine gives.** The brine leaves the exchanger at no less than the
  return temperature plus the approach. A low return temperature lets the brine cool further and
  gives more heat per m3 produced, up to any limit on brine cooling the case states.
- **The flow in the network.** For a given power the flow is inversely proportional to the
  supply-return difference, so pumping power and pipe size fall as the difference grows.

Lower network temperatures (as in 4th-generation district heating) raise the heat taken from a
low-temperature source and lower losses [paper: Lund et al. 2014]. Where the return temperature
is a design choice of the team (not fixed by the case), choose it low enough to cool the brine
deeply, and high enough that buildings can still be heated with their existing emitters; record
the choice and its reason.

## 6.2 Cascading: using the brine more than once

A cascade passes the brine through several users in order of falling temperature: the hottest
service first, then lower-temperature services on the cooler brine. The Lindal diagram classifies
direct uses by the temperature they need [textbook: Lindal 1973, reproduced in Stober and Bucher
2013]. In a heating and cooling plant common cascades are:

  the heat pump then cools the brine further (its evaporator on the brine) and lifts that heat to the
  supply temperature. This raises the heat per m3 and keeps the brine cooling within its limit.
- **Absorption chiller drive, then heating**: the hottest water drives the chiller (it needs a high
  drive temperature, 7.2) and its outlet still heats a lower-temperature service.
- **Series of exchangers on the network**: the coolest return water meets the coolest brine first.

## 4. Prices, currency, price year and escalation

### 4.1 Nominal and real money

- **Nominal** (current) money: amounts as they will be paid, including inflation.
- **Real** (constant) money: amounts in the purchasing power of one base year, the **price year**.

A real analysis uses real prices and a **real** discount rate; a nominal analysis uses escalated
prices and a **nominal** rate. The two give the same NPV when done consistently (Fisher relation:
`1 + i_nominal = (1 + i_real)(1 + inflation)`). Mixing them, for example real prices with a
nominal rate, undervalues every future year.

matches.text:
An operational assessment of a geothermal plant usually reports scope 1 and scope 2. Embodied
emissions of drilling and equipment (scope 3) are a life-cycle question; include them only with a
life-cycle source.

### 9.2 Direct CO2 from produced gas and combustion

Deep brines can carry dissolved gas (CO2, CH4, N2, H2S). When the gas comes out of solution in the
degasser:

- the **CO2** in it is released to the air unless it is reinjected or captured;
- the **CH4** is flared, burnt for heat or power, or vented. Combustion turns it into CO2
  (44/16 = 2.75 kg CO2 per kg CH4 burnt, from the molar masses; **derived**). Flaring is not
  complete: the unburnt part is released as methane (gemini's flare states a combustion
  efficiency of 0.98, cited to US EPA AP-42 section 13.5).

Bought gas burnt in boilers adds its combustion CO2, from its composition.

### 9.3 Methane and global warming potentials (IPCC AR6)

Methane released unburnt is converted to CO2-equivalent with a global warming potential (GWP):

`CO2e = m_CO2 + GWP_CH4 · m_CH4`

Variable O&M scales with the energy produced: wear, consumables, part of the maintenance. DEA
version 0019 gives a plant variable O&M of 3.07 EUR/MWh of heat (EUR 2025) for its geothermal
sheets 45.1.b and 45.3 (catalogue row `opex-variable-dea-2025`, status *verified*; the row notes
that it includes chemical treatment). Do not add a separate chemical cost on top of a variable
O&M that already includes it.

### 3.3 Energy bought: electricity and gas

The largest running cost of a geothermal heat pump plant is usually electricity: ESPs, injection
pumps, circulation pumps, heat pumps and compression chillers. Gas is bought for peak boilers when
the produced gas does not suffice.

- Bill = energy bought in each step × price in that step, summed over the year.
- Price the energy at the **delivered price paid by the plant**: the consumption band, the network
  charges and the non-recoverable taxes that apply (chapter 10).
- For gas, state the heating value convention. Eurostat quotes gas prices per kWh of **gross**
  calorific value; a model that counts fuel on the **lower** heating value must convert, or the
  bill is off by the ratio of the two (about 10 % for natural gas; a general figure, check it for
  the gas in question). gemini prices gas per energy of its lower heating value (schema of
  `economics.energy.gas`).
- Co-produced gas burnt on site costs nothing to buy, but its combustion emits CO2 (chapter 9).

### 3.4 Chemicals and waste

matches.text:
- **Keep it in solution**: hold the surface loop above the bubble point (pressurised loop),
  inject the gas back with the brine. Simpler, no gas to handle, but needs pressure margin
  everywhere, and the gas never earns anything.
- **Separate it**: degas at a controlled pressure (5.2), then use or dispose of the gas (5.5). Needed
  when the gas content is high or the gas has value as fuel; it produces emissions that must be
  counted (5.6).

## 5.2 Degassers and separators

A degasser (gas separator) lets the free gas leave the liquid in a vessel at a set pressure. Its
design values are the vessel pressure (or pressure drop) and the separation efficiency. In gemini
the `Degasser` removes a share `separation_efficiency` of the free gas and applies a pressure loss;
dissolved gas that does not come out at the vessel pressure stays in the liquid (Henry's law and
residence time are not modelled) [gemini: `gemini/modules/treatment/degasser.py`].

Place the degasser upstream of the heat exchanger so that the exchanger sees liquid only, and after
the production wells are joined, so that one vessel serves all doublets. A lower vessel pressure
releases more gas but makes scaling more likely; a design without PVT data cannot predict the
dissolved share and must say so.

- **Burn before you flare.** If a boiler or CHP needs heat anyway, the co-produced gas is free fuel.
  Size the boiler's base fuel use to the gas available, top up with grid gas, and send only the
  surplus to the flare. In gemini a `GasMakeup` offers the co-produced gas to the burner first,
  draws the shortfall from the `GasGrid` and sends the surplus to its `excess_out`, usually a
  `Flare` [gemini: `gemini/modules/piping/gasmakeup.py`; the `Boiler` and `CHP` burn the
  co-produced gas first, `boiler.py`, `chp.py`].
- **Know the fuel value.** The heating value of the co-produced gas depends on its methane share.
  For pure methane the lower heating value is about 50.0 MJ/kg, about 35.8 MJ/Nm3 [textbook: standard
  combustion tables; the per-Nm3 figure is derived with a methane density of 0.717 kg/Nm3]. CO2 in
  the gas adds no fuel value.
- **A CHP must be able to sell or use its power**, and needs enough running hours; with little
  gas the engine is small and its specific cost high (6.6).

matches.text:
Fouling of the exchanger lowers its UA over time; design for the fouled state and monitor it (gemini
reports a fouling diagnostic against `fouling_threshold` [gemini: `heatexchanger.py`]).

## 5.4 Sand and filters

Weakly consolidated sandstones produce fines and sand, which erode pumps and clog injectors.
Remedies, from the well outward: sand control in the completion, a **desander** (hydrocyclone) at
the surface, and **filters** before the exchanger and before the injector. A hydrocyclone's
pressure loss is of the order of 1 bar at design flow and its efficiency depends on particle size
against its cut size [textbook: Svarovsky 2000, as cited in gemini
`gemini/modules/treatment/desander.py`]; both are design-specific values to source from the
vendor. The sand load comes from the case (`site.fluid.sand_concentration`); the removed sand is
waste with a disposal price.

gemini models `Desander`, `Filter` (with a clogging pressure drop) and `WasteGrid` for the removed
solids.

matches.name: knowledge/handbook-design.md
matches.text:
In gemini the `HeatExchanger` takes `thermal_conductance` (UA), `arrangement`, nominal pressure
drops and flows; its role quantities are `duty` and `approach` [gemini: `gemini/plants/roles.py`].
Note that gemini's `size` does not size the exchanger: it keeps the plant's UA and lists it as
unchanged [gemini: `gemini/study/size.py`], so check the approach in the results (11.7) and set UA
yourself.

## 6.2 Cascading: using the brine more than once

A cascade passes the brine through several users in order of falling temperature: the hottest
service first, then lower-temperature services on the cooler brine. The Lindal diagram classifies
direct uses by the temperature they need [textbook: Lindal 1973, reproduced in Stober and Bucher
2013]. In a heating and cooling plant common cascades are:

- **Exchanger, then heat pump on the brine**: the exchanger takes the heat the brine gives directly;
  the heat pump then cools the brine further (its evaporator on the brine) and lifts that heat to the
  supply temperature. This raises the heat per m3 and keeps the brine cooling within its limit.
- **Absorption chiller drive, then heating**: the hottest water drives the chiller (it needs a high
  drive temperature, 7.2) and its outlet still heats a lower-temperature service.
- **Series of exchangers on the network**: the coolest return water meets the coolest brine first.

Order users so each takes the brine at the temperature it needs and no higher.

matches.name: knowledge/handbook-economics.md
matches.text:
- **A heater that drives another unit.** A boiler (or the geothermal water) that heats the
  generator of an absorption chiller sends part of its heat into the chiller, not to the heating
  users. The heating users' heat by source is therefore not `heat_delivered − boiler_heat`.
- **A heat pump.** Its heat output is the heat it lifts from the brine plus its compressor work
  (electricity). The brine gave the output minus that work: output / COP of it is electricity.
- **A CHP.** Its fuel gives electricity and heat; the heat to the users is its heat output, the
  electricity is sold or offsets grid power.

Rules:

1. Take the split by source from gemini (its per-service coverage: geothermal, backup and short,
   as the result's coverage gives it), never by subtracting one unit's output from a total.
2. When no tool gives the split you need, say so; do not derive it.
3. For a heat pump plant, state the brine's heat and the compressor's electricity apart.

Invented example: heating demand 100 000 MWh/yr. The boiler makes 40 000 MWh, of which 12 000
drive the absorption chiller and 28 000 go to heating. Geothermal heat to the heating users is
100 000 − 28 000 = 72 000 MWh, not 100 000 − 40 000 = 60 000 (20 % too low). A heat pump that
delivers 50 000 MWh at a seasonal COP of 4 takes 12 500 MWh of electricity and 37 500 MWh from
the brine; "50 000 MWh from geothermal" overstates the brine by a third.

matches.text:
- **Whether the brine can supply the heat directly.** The brine must be hotter than the supply
  temperature by at least the approach of the exchanger (6.1). If not, a heat pump, a boiler or
  deeper wells must close the gap (6.3).
- **How much heat a kilogram of brine gives.** The brine leaves the exchanger at no less than the
  return temperature plus the approach. A low return temperature lets the brine cool further and
  gives more heat per m3 produced, up to any limit on brine cooling the case states.
- **The flow in the network.** For a given power the flow is inversely proportional to the
  supply-return difference, so pumping power and pipe size fall as the difference grows.

Lower network temperatures (as in 4th-generation district heating) raise the heat taken from a
low-temperature source and lower losses [paper: Lund et al. 2014]. Where the return temperature
is a design choice of the team (not fixed by the case), choose it low enough to cool the brine
deeply, and high enough that buildings can still be heated with their existing emitters; record
the choice and its reason.

1. **Is there a project plant that fits the services?** Start from it (`read_plant(project_plant=...)`).
2. **Which services?** Heating only: A, G or H. Heating and cooling: B, C, D, E, F or I.
3. **How hot is the brine against the heating supply?** Take the reservoir temperature at the
   design depth from the case's gradient (3.1) and compare with the heating supply T_s, the return
   T_r and an exchanger approach (6.1, 6.3):
   - T_brine ≥ T_s + approach: direct use (A, C, E);
   - T_r + approach < T_brine < T_s + approach: heat pump boost (B, D), or deeper wells (3.6);
   - T_brine ≤ T_r + approach: a heat pump on the brine only (H).
4. **How is cold made?** Brine above an absorption chiller's minimum drive temperature plus the
   approach in summer: absorption is a candidate (C, D, E). Otherwise, or with a high chilled-water
   supply (20 °C and up) and affordable electricity: compression (B) (7.8).
5. **Is there co-produced gas?** Substantial gas: burn it before you flare (F, G; 5.5). Some gas:

6. **More than one sensible answer?** One superstructure (optional modules, `choices`), or a

The same brief must give the same requirements every time. Write them by this procedure, not
freely:

   one requirement. A geoscientist proposes, the lead decides.
2. **Merge on `on` + `quantity`.** Before `set_case`, group all proposals by `on`, `quantity`,

3. **Shape from §6.9.** Take `over`, `when` and `unit` from the pattern table, never chosen anew.

   `<quantity>_floor` (`min`), `<quantity>_exact` (`min` = `max`); for days of operation
   `running_time_limit`; for a count `<role>_count`; for demand met `heat_delivered` and
   `cold_delivered`. Stable names keep the verdict, the comparison of designs and the report
   readable across runs.
5. **Tolerances from one source, all of them.** When an assumptions document of the case lists
   tolerances, take every one of its rows (demand met, ratios), as written; otherwise propose each
   in the one question (§6.8). Never a tolerance in one run and an exact value in the next.

## 7.1 The test

**Who decides it?** A third party (client, organiser, regulator, nature): a case value or a
rule. The team: a design freedom. A freedom is never asked of the user as a missing value and
never written into the case; a bound on it is a requirement.

## 7.2 Typical freedoms

| Freedom | Lives in | Bound in the case |
|---|---|---|
| well depth | plant `params.depth` | none; the reservoir stays a case value |
| number of doublets | plant `size.doublets` | `doublet.count` requirement |
| flows, set points, controls | plant | flow range requirement |
| units and sizes (heat pump, boiler, chiller, CHP, store) | plant | none |
| backup policy | plant `params.backup` | demand-met requirement |
| associated gas handling (flare, boiler, CHP) | plant | emission rules, if any |

## 7.3 Return temperatures

The one team choice that sits in the case. A return temperature no file gives is a design
choice within the case's limits, not a value the design waits for: never ask the user
to supply it and never stop for it. Propose it in the one question:
`<path> = <value> <unit> | design choice, the brief leaves it to the team | <reason>`, taking
the value of an assumptions document of the case when one gives it. On approval record it with
`source: "agent"`, `confirmed: true`, `citation: {"origin": "design choice"}`.

## 7.4 A case change from the design team

The design team never changes the case. It hands over `case change needed: <path>: <why>`; the
case lead changes it and the user approves (`case_changes`, skill `setting-the-case`).

{'name': 'knowledge/handbook-case.md', 'section': {'number': '6', 'title': '6. Requirements', 'start': 22178, 'size': 8815}, 'start': 0, 'total': 8815, 'text': '# 6. Requirements

## 6.1 What a requirement is

A rule of a third party on the outcome: a quantity of a role, with its band
(`gemini/gemini/case/requirement.py`). It applies to every unit of the role on its own, and
gemini's verdict judges it (`check_results`). Never a design choice ("use two doublets"), a set
point the team chooses, or a site value.

## 6.2 Qualities of a good requirement

| Quality (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018) | In a case |
|---|---|
| necessary | it comes from the brief or a third party, not from the team's preference |
| unambiguous | one reading: which unit, which steps, which quantity |
| complete | both ends where the brief gives both; the steps it holds in |
| singular | one rule per requirement; a range with two ends is one rule |
| feasible | some plant can meet it; one no plant can meet is a flaw to ask about |
| verifiable | gemini can judge it: a role and quantity of §6.4 |
| traceable | its `name` and its source page recorded with it |

## 6.3 Keys

`{name, on, quantity, unit, over, when, min, max}` (`KEYS`).

| Key | Rule |
|---|---|
| `name` | unique, snake_case (`production_flow_range`) |
| `on` | a role (§6.4) |
| `quantity` | a quantity of that role |
| `over` | per-step quantities only: how the run is read (§6.5); refused on a property or window quantity |
| `when` | per-step quantities only: `always` or `running`; every step when absent (§6.6) |
| `min`, `max` | at least one; exact rule: `min` = `max` (`equals` is refused) |
| `unit` | present only when the bounds have a dimension; over `duration`, a duration (`d`, `h`) |

## 6.4 Roles and quantities

From `gemini/gemini/plants/roles.py` (`TABLE`; `gm.plants.roles()`). A role is read from the
plant's wiring, never from a module name. *Property* and *window* quantities take no `over` and
no `when`.

| Role | Quantities |
|---|---|
| `doublet` | `production_flow`, `brine_cooling`, `production_temperature`, `injection_temperature`, `pump_power`, `pump_efficiency` (property), `intake_pressure`, `intake_gas_fraction`, `reinjection_ratio`, `count` (property), `wellhead_pressure` |
| `heat_pump` | `cop`, `lift`, `heat_output` |
| `boiler` | `fuel_input`, `heat_output` |
| `chp` | `power_output`, `heat_output` |
| `chiller` | `cop`, `cold_output` |
| `heat_exchanger` | `duty`, `approach` |
| `heating_supply` | `temperature`, `unmet`, `unmet_share` (window) |
| `cooling_supply` | `temperature`, `unmet`, `unmet_share` (window) |
| `plant` | `electricity_bought`, `gas_bought`, `heat_surplus`, `co2`, `gas_burned` |

`reinjection_ratio`: injected over produced liquid volume flow. `count`: number of doublets.
`unmet_share`: unmet over demanded energy of the service over the whole period. `co2` of `plant`:
CO2-equivalent mass per step, so `over: sum` is the run's mass.

## 6.5 `over`: how the run is read

| `over` | Judges | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `each` | every counted step | a cap or band per step (flow range, brine cooling, temperature) |
| `sum` | the sum | a total (CO2 of the year, energy bought) |
| `mean` | the mean | an average limit |
| `max`, `min` | the extreme | a peak as one figure |
| `duration` | total time of the steps where `when` holds; bounds are durations | days or hours of operation |

## 6.6 `when`: which steps count

- `running`: steps where the unit carries flow. Use for anything that holds while equipment
  runs: flow bands, brine cooling, a fixed supply temperature. An idle loop sits at its return
  temperature; `always` would fail a correct plant.
- `always`: every step, running or not; rare (a rating that may never be exceeded).

## 6.7 Bounds

- cap: `max`; floor: `min`; a range with both ends: ONE requirement with both;
- exact: `min` = `max`;
- fraction, share, ratio, efficiency: no unit (70 % is `0.7`);
- days of operation: `over: duration`, `when: running`, unit `d`;
- number of units: `{on: doublet, quantity: count, min, max}`, no `over`, `when`, `unit`.

## 6.8 Tolerances

A brief that says "the demand shall be met" or "equal volumes are reinjected" gives no
tolerance, and a simulation never meets them exactly. Propose one in the one question, named as
an assumption with its reason:

- demand met: one `unmet_share` requirement per supply, a small `max` such as a percent of the period's energy;
- an exact ratio: a narrow band around it (such as ± 0.001 % of the ratio).

Too loose passes a design the client rejects; too tight fails one on numerical noise.

## 6.9 Brief text to requirement

Placeholders A, B, X, N, E, M come from the brief.

| Brief says | Requirement |
|---|---|
| "Flow per well between A and B m³/h" | `on: doublet, quantity: production_flow, over: each, when: running, min: A, max: B, unit: m3/h` |
| "Brine cooled by at most X K" | `on: doublet, quantity: brine_cooling, over: each, when: running, max: X, unit: K` |
| "A doublet operates at most N days a year" | `on: doublet, quantity: production_flow, over: duration, when: running, max: N, unit: d` |
| "Pump efficiency E %" | `on: doublet, quantity: pump_efficiency, min: E/100, max: E/100` (written as the fraction) |
| "All produced water is reinjected" | `on: doublet, quantity: reinjection_ratio, over: each, when: running`, narrow band (§6.8) |
| "1 to 3 doublets" | `on: doublet, quantity: count, min: 1, max: 3` |
| "The heat demand is met" | `on: heating_supply, quantity: unmet_share, max: <tolerance>` |
| "Supply at T °C, fixed" | case value `demand.*.supply_temperature`; a temperature requirement, if written, is `when: running` |
| "Annual emissions below M t" | `on: plant, quantity: co2, over: sum, max: M, unit: t` |

A limit on one source's availability (a doublet's days) is that source's, never the system's:
the system meets the demand on every day.

## 6.10 Rules gemini cannot express

A noise, land-use or permit rule, or one on a role gemini lacks, goes in the case's `about` and
is named as open in the handover and the report. Never dropped, never forced into a requirement
that means something else.

## 6.11 Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| `when: always` on a supply temperature | `when: running` |
| two requirements for one range | one with `min` and `max` |
| `count` for days, or `duration` for units | duration for time, count for units |
| `unit: "%"` on an efficiency | a fraction, no unit |
| a team preference as a requirement | it belongs to the design brief |
| a doublet's availability read as the system's | system demand met every day |
| two proposals on the same `on` and `quantity` (`min_stable_flow` 50 and `max_production_flow` 300) kept apart when merging | merge them into one requirement with `min` and `max` (§6.12) |
| an exact ratio as `min: 1, max: 1` | a narrow band from the tolerance source (§6.8): an exact 1 fails on round-off |
| a temperature difference (`brine_cooling`, `approach`, `lift`) in `degC` | `K`, the unit of a difference |
| a rule a source marks conditional ("only if the design checks it") written as a requirement | left out of the case; named in the handover for the design team |
| a requirement the brief does not state, added from a reference or a habit | only rules of the brief, the client or an assumptions document of the case |

## 6.12 The same requirements every run

The same brief must give the same requirements every time. Write them by this procedure, not
freely:

1. **One row per rule.** List each rule sentence of the brief (§1.2) with its page; one rule is
   one requirement. A geoscientist proposes, the lead decides.
2. **Merge on `on` + `quantity`.** Before `set_case`, group all proposals by `on`, `quantity`,
   `over` and `when`. Two in one group are one rule: one requirement with the `min` of one and
   the `max` of the other. Two different values for the same bound are a disagreement (§1.4).
3. **Shape from §6.9.** Take `over`, `when` and `unit` from the pattern table, never chosen anew.
4. **Names by pattern.** `<quantity>_range` (both bounds), `<quantity>_limit` (`max`),
   `<quantity>_floor` (`min`), `<quantity>_exact` (`min` = `max`); for days of operation
   `running_time_limit`; for a count `<role>_count`; for demand met `heat_delivered` and
   `cold_delivered`. Stable names keep the verdict, the comparison of designs and the report
   readable across runs.
5. **Tolerances from one source, all of them.** When an assumptions document of the case lists
   tolerances, take every one of its rows (demand met, ratios), as written; otherwise propose each
   in the one question (§6.8). Never a tolerance in one run and an exact value in the next.
6. **Count and compare.** Count the requirements against the rule list of step 1; when an
   assumptions document or a reference case of the same brief lists its requirements, compare
   name by name and name every difference with its reason in the handover.

### 5.2 Present value, annuity factor and capital recovery factor

Present value of an amount `F` paid at the end of year `t` at rate `r`:

`PV = F / (1 + r)^t`

Annuity (present value) factor of a constant yearly amount over `n` years, paid at the end of
years 1 to `n`:

`A(r, n) = Σ_{t=1..n} 1 / (1 + r)^t = (1 − (1 + r)^−n) / r`, and `A = n` when `r = 0`.

Capital recovery factor (CRF), the yearly payment that repays 1 unit of capital over `n` years:

`CRF(r, n) = 1 / A(r, n) = r (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1)`

**Handbook: defining an energy-supply case** (`knowledge/handbook-case.md`)

How to turn a brief and data files into a complete, sourced case for a geothermal heating and
cooling plant in gemini. For the case lead, the geoscientists and any reviewer of a case.

- **Cite as** `knowledge/handbook-case.md §<section>` (for example `§6.5`).
- **Read by section**, never whole: `read_knowledge(name="knowledge/handbook-case.md",
  section="0")`. Chapter 0 is the short version of the whole handbook; read it first, then only
  the sections it points to.
- **Source of truth.** Keys, units, roles and quantities are gemini's (`gemini/gemini/case/`,
  `gemini/gemini/plants/roles.py`, `gemini/gemini/units/inputs.py`, gemini 0.6.17). When this
  handbook and `describe_case(path)` differ, `describe_case` wins.
- **Not here.** How to call a tool: skill `setting-the-case` (cases), `finding-sources`
  (files, Knowledge), `connectors` (servers), `calculator`, `gemini-units`. Economics:
  `knowledge/handbook-economics.md`. Plant design: `knowledge/handbook-design.md`. Report:
  `knowledge/handbook-report.md`.
- **Numbers in this handbook** are definitions, examples of a pattern, or values of the
  worked example (chapter 12). None is a value for another case.

## 10.4 Validation

- A rejected `set_case` stores nothing and names each path; fix them all and resend the SAME full
  call, never a files-only call.
- `case_incomplete` lists every missing path at once.
- `missing_value` (or `missing_assumption` under `economics`) names the path a run needs.
- `plants_need` lists case values the project's plants still lack: each goes into the follow-up
  question (§8.4) before the case is called complete.

## 10.5 The user's case and later changes

The project's case, or a chat's first case, is the case the user gave. Every later change,
economics included, waits for the user's approval (`case_changes`, `accept_case`).

# Handbook of Techno-Economic and Environmental Assessment of Geothermal Heating and Cooling Plants

How to cost a geothermal heating and cooling plant, put a carbon footprint on it, and use both to
choose between designs. General for any case; chapter 17 works a full example on invented
numbers. Checked against gemini 0.6.17 and the cost catalogue `knowledge/data-economics.csv` (157
rows) on 2026-11-05.

Cite as `knowledge/handbook-economics.md` with the section (for example
`knowledge/handbook-economics.md §6.3`). Every section stands alone: read the one you need
(`read_knowledge` with its number). Chapter 0 is the short version for agents.

This handbook explains no tool. Running costs, sensitivity and uncertainty: skill `economics`.
Setting economics in a case (`ask_economics`, `set_case`): skill `setting-the-case`. Defining the
rest of the case: `knowledge/handbook-case.md`. Reporting the numbers:
`knowledge/handbook-report.md`.

---

## 0. Quick reference for the agents

### 0.1 Rules that hold in every section

   it needs, the case keys it owns and what the case already holds.
4. **Merge.** Merge the findings into one list of values with their sources. Save nothing yet.
5. **Search the gaps.** For each missing value: Knowledge (assumptions document first), then a
   connector (§0.3, §8.1).
6. **Ask once.** ONE confirmation question with every value that did not come from the user's
   files, every flaw, and every agent choice (§8.4). Nothing that needs approval is saved before
   `approve all`.
7. **Set once.** ONE `set_case` with the file and user values and the approved values (§10).
8. **Follow-up, only if needed.** When that `set_case` returns `plants_need` paths or unit names it
   mapped (`converted`), ONE more `ask_user` with only those (§8.4, §10.4).
9. **Economics once.** ONE `ask_economics` question (skill `setting-the-case`;
   `knowledge/handbook-economics.md`).
10. **Check and hand over.** `read_case` again, then the checklist §11.2.

   `running_time_limit`; for a count `<role>_count`; for demand met `heat_delivered` and
   `cold_delivered`. Stable names keep the verdict, the comparison of designs and the report
   readable across runs.
5. **Tolerances from one source, all of them.** When an assumptions document of the case lists
   tolerances, take every one of its rows (demand met, ratios), as written; otherwise propose each
   in the one question (§6.8). Never a tolerance in one run and an exact value in the next.
6. **Count and compare.** Count the requirements against the rule list of step 1; when an
   assumptions document or a reference case of the same brief lists its requirements, compare

failed, or none could be judged), `failed_step` (rows that failed or were skipped),
`numerical` (a mass or energy residual above tolerance, a loop that did not converge) and
`bound` (an output outside its module's limits or operating limits). A result with a failed step
is not feasible, whatever its totals say.

is `{name, role, unit_path, quantity, passed, value, limit, worst_step}`, one per unit and
requirement, plus the supply temperature of each service, checked in the steps the service
runs.

matches.text:
- `feasible`: true when there is no reason.
- `reasons`, each with a `kind`:
  - `requirement`: a requirement of the case failed (or could not be judged);
  - `failed_step`: steps of the run that failed or were skipped: a simulation problem in the plant;
  - `numerical`: a mass or energy residual above tolerance, or a loop that did not converge;
  - `bound`: an output outside a module's declared limits or past an operating limit (an ESP's
    intake pressure or gas fraction).
  Each reason has a `name`, a `message`, and when known `path`, `value`, `limit`, `worst_step`.
- `requirements`: one check per unit of each requirement; `failures`: failed steps by module and
  code.

Read the worst step: it tells when (the peak day, a zero-demand day) and where (which module). Then
read the module's results around that step (`read_result`) before changing anything. An
`unmet_share` of a run with failed steps is undecided (`passed` null), not failed: fix the failed
steps first [gemini: `docs/CHANGELOG.md` 0.6.13, QA-104].

matches.text:
- `running`: steps where the unit carries flow. Use for anything that holds while equipment
  runs: flow bands, brine cooling, a fixed supply temperature. An idle loop sits at its return
  temperature; `always` would fail a correct plant.
- `always`: every step, running or not; rare (a rating that may never be exceeded).

## 6.7 Bounds

- cap: `max`; floor: `min`; a range with both ends: ONE requirement with both;
- exact: `min` = `max`;
- fraction, share, ratio, efficiency: no unit (70 % is `0.7`);
- days of operation: `over: duration`, `when: running`, unit `d`;
- number of units: `{on: doublet, quantity: count, min, max}`, no `over`, `when`, `unit`.

## 6.8 Tolerances

A brief that says "the demand shall be met" or "equal volumes are reinjected" gives no
tolerance, and a simulation never meets them exactly. Propose one in the one question, named as
an assumption with its reason:

- demand met: one `unmet_share` requirement per supply, a small `max` such as a percent of the period's energy;
- an exact ratio: a narrow band around it (such as ± 0.001 % of the ratio).

Too loose passes a design the client rejects; too tight fails one on numerical noise.

## 6.9 Brief text to requirement

Placeholders A, B, X, N, E, M come from the brief.

# 3 The subsurface

This chapter gives the reservoir values a design needs and how they follow from depth: temperature,
pressure, productivity, drawdown, thermal breakthrough. Most of them are properties of the site
(the case) and only the depth and well design are choices.

## 3.1 Reservoir temperature from the gradient

In conductive settings the temperature rises roughly linearly with depth:

T(z) = T_surface + G · z

with T_surface the mean surface (or reference) temperature and G the geothermal gradient. Typical
continental gradients are of the order of 25 to 35 K/km; sedimentary basins with thick insulating
cover can be higher [textbook: Stober and Bucher 2013]. The gradient of a site comes from the case
(measured wells, maps), never from a typical value.

## 3.2 Reservoir pressure at depth

In a normally pressured aquifer the pore pressure is close to hydrostatic: p(z) ≈ ρ g z (gauge, with
the water table at the surface). From a reference pressure p_ref at depth z_ref:

p(z) = p_ref + ρ g (z − z_ref)

[gemini: `gemini/physics/ground.py`, `reservoir_pressure`]. gemini applies it: the case gives the
pressure at `site.reservoir.reference_depth`, and a doublet designed at another depth gets the
pressure at its own depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `_doublets`]. Therefore **change the
plant's depth, not the case's reference depth**, to explore deeper wells: changing the reference
depth without changing the reference pressure describes a different reservoir (QA-119).

## 3.3 Productivity and injectivity

The productivity index (PI) relates the flow to the drawdown, Q = PI · (p_res − p_wf). For steady
radial Darcy flow into a well [textbook: Dake 1978]:

PI = 2π k h / ( μ · ( ln(r_e / r_w) + S ) )

with k the permeability, h the net thickness, μ the brine viscosity, r_e the drainage radius, r_w
the wellbore radius and S the skin. The injectivity index (II) has the same form for the injector.

## 3.2 Reservoir pressure at depth

In a normally pressured aquifer the pore pressure is close to hydrostatic: p(z) ≈ ρ g z (gauge, with
the water table at the surface). From a reference pressure p_ref at depth z_ref:

p(z) = p_ref + ρ g (z − z_ref)

[gemini: `gemini/physics/ground.py`, `reservoir_pressure`]. gemini applies it: the case gives the
pressure at `site.reservoir.reference_depth`, and a doublet designed at another depth gets the
pressure at its own depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `_doublets`]. Therefore **change the
plant's depth, not the case's reference depth**, to explore deeper wells: changing the reference
depth without changing the reference pressure describes a different reservoir (QA-119).

## 3.3 Productivity and injectivity

The productivity index (PI) relates the flow to the drawdown, Q = PI · (p_res − p_wf). For steady
radial Darcy flow into a well [textbook: Dake 1978]:

PI = 2π k h / ( μ · ( ln(r_e / r_w) + S ) )

with k the permeability, h the net thickness, μ the brine viscosity, r_e the drainage radius, r_w
the wellbore radius and S the skin. The injectivity index (II) has the same form for the injector.

This chapter gives the reservoir values a design needs and how they follow from depth: temperature,

## 3.1 Reservoir temperature from the gradient

In conductive settings the temperature rises roughly linearly with depth:

T(z) = T_surface + G · z

with T_surface the mean surface (or reference) temperature and G the geothermal gradient. Typical
continental gradients are of the order of 25 to 35 K/km; sedimentary basins with thick insulating
cover can be higher [textbook: Stober and Bucher 2013]. The gradient of a site comes from the case
(measured wells, maps), never from a typical value.

  days a doublet either runs at its minimum and the surplus heat must go somewhere (it cannot), or it
  stops and another unit covers the day. Several doublets give finer steps.
- **Heat pump and chiller**: below a minimum part load the compressor stops or cycles [gemini:
  `heatpump.py`, `minimum_part_load`]. A machine sized for the peak runs below its minimum on mild
  days; two smaller machines cover a wider range.
- **Boiler**: modulates over a wide range but loses efficiency with frequent starts; not modelled
  in daily steps.
- **Sorption chillers** need their drive temperature at every load (7.2).

Check minimum loads against the lowest demand of each service (2.1). When the lowest heat demand
is below one doublet's minimum heat (minimum flow times c_p times brine cooling), the doublet will
cycle off on those days; that is fine if the backup covers them (8.5).

matches.text:
The produced (wellhead) temperature is a little lower than the reservoir temperature because the
brine loses heat on the way up; the loss is larger at low flow and in thin wells. gemini computes
it with the wells' heat transfer coefficient (`heat_transfer_coefficient`, 0.7).

## 3.2 Reservoir pressure at depth

In a normally pressured aquifer the pore pressure is close to hydrostatic: p(z) ≈ ρ g z (gauge, with
the water table at the surface). From a reference pressure p_ref at depth z_ref:

p(z) = p_ref + ρ g (z − z_ref)

[gemini: `gemini/physics/ground.py`, `reservoir_pressure`]. gemini applies it: the case gives the
pressure at `site.reservoir.reference_depth`, and a doublet designed at another depth gets the
pressure at its own depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `_doublets`]. Therefore **change the
plant's depth, not the case's reference depth**, to explore deeper wells: changing the reference
depth without changing the reference pressure describes a different reservoir (QA-119).

## 3.3 Productivity and injectivity

The productivity index (PI) relates the flow to the drawdown, Q = PI · (p_res − p_wf). For steady
radial Darcy flow into a well [textbook: Dake 1978]:

PI = 2π k h / ( μ · ( ln(r_e / r_w) + S ) )

with k the permeability, h the net thickness, μ the brine viscosity, r_e the drainage radius, r_w
the wellbore radius and S the skin. The injectivity index (II) has the same form for the injector.

# 3 The subsurface

This chapter gives the reservoir values a design needs and how they follow from depth: temperature,
pressure, productivity, drawdown, thermal breakthrough. Most of them are properties of the site
(the case) and only the depth and well design are choices.

## 3.1 Reservoir temperature from the gradient

In conductive settings the temperature rises roughly linearly with depth:

T(z) = T_surface + G · z

with T_surface the mean surface (or reference) temperature and G the geothermal gradient. Typical
continental gradients are of the order of 25 to 35 K/km; sedimentary basins with thick insulating
cover can be higher [textbook: Stober and Bucher 2013]. The gradient of a site comes from the case
(measured wells, maps), never from a typical value.

In gemini the plant states only the depth; the case holds `site.ground.gradient` and
`site.ground.surface_temperature`, and the run derives the reservoir temperature at the plant's
depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `gemini/plants/doublet.py`].

- **The saved case is the user's.** Its values are `source: user`: never ask the user for a value
  they saved, and never ask them to approve it again (§8.7).
- **Every earlier read is stale.** After a load (`set_case(source="project")`) or any `set_case`,
  results of `read_case`, `case_changes` and briefs written before it no longer hold. Read the case
  again (`read_case`) before a brief, a question or a claim, and quote values only from that read.
- **The case beats the brief.** When a brief says one value and `read_case` shows another, the case
  is right: report the difference to whoever wrote the brief; do not ask the user.
- **What changed** is the difference between the case before the load and the case after it
  (path, `before -> after`), named in the handover and on the card (§8.8). `case_changes` compares
  with the case the user gave, so after a load of the user's own case it may be empty: that means
  "nothing to approve", not "nothing changed".
- The next step is the design team's: simulate and check the current design on the new case. A
  case lead step is needed only when gemini names a missing value.

How to turn a brief and data files into a complete, sourced case for a geothermal heating and
cooling plant in gemini. For the case lead, the geoscientists and any reviewer of a case.

- **Cite as** `knowledge/handbook-case.md §<section>` (for example `§6.5`).

# 10. How gemini handles a case

## 10.1 Sections and files

Order of `case.json`: header (`format`, `kind`, `name`), `time`, `initial_state`, `site`,
`demand`, `utilities`, `economics`, `requirements` (`gemini/gemini/case/case.py`). A series is
`{file, column, unit}` plus optional `range` and `time_zone`; the data file is given to the case
by name, never retyped. Values the user types become a file through `save_profile`. A stateful
module (a store) has no default `initial_state`.

## 10.2 Derived keys: never set by hand

| Key | gemini derives it from |
|---|---|
| `site.reservoir.temperature` (when not measured) | ground surface temperature, gradient, depth |
| pressure at another depth | reservoir pressure, hydrostatic column |
| `site.air.pressure` from `{elevation}` | ISA standard atmosphere (ISO 2533:1975), set by `set_case` |

## 6.2 Cascading: using the brine more than once

A cascade passes the brine through several users in order of falling temperature: the hottest
service first, then lower-temperature services on the cooler brine. The Lindal diagram classifies
direct uses by the temperature they need [textbook: Lindal 1973, reproduced in Stober and Bucher

  drive temperature, 7.2) and its outlet still heats a lower-temperature service.

## 4. Prices, currency, price year and escalation

### 4.1 Nominal and real money

- **Nominal** (current) money: amounts as they will be paid, including inflation.
- **Real** (constant) money: amounts in the purchasing power of one base year, the **price year**.

A real analysis uses real prices and a **real** discount rate; a nominal analysis uses escalated
prices and a **nominal** rate. The two give the same NPV when done consistently (Fisher relation:
`1 + i_nominal = (1 + i_real)(1 + inflation)`). Mixing them, for example real prices with a
nominal rate, undervalues every future year.

matches.text:
- standard stages: about 18.75 % free gas by volume (75 % for gas-handler stages, divided by four)
  [catalogue: Baker Hughes, Ace Plus gas handler pumps];
- a stricter rule of thumb of 10 % for a standard pump is quoted from Takacs (2009) but was not
  verified at the book.

An upper-bound estimate of the free gas fraction treats all gas as free (no solubility) and ideal
[derived, Appendix A.6]:

α ≈ GLR · (p_n / p) · (T / T_n) / (1 + GLR · (p_n / p) · (T / T_n))

With GLR 0.5 Nm3/m3 and 95 °C at the intake (invented) this gives about 6 % at 10 bar(a) and
about 12 % at 5 bar(a) [derived]. Two consequences:

- the gas limit and the intake pressure limit are linked: deeper, hotter, higher-flow designs pull
  the intake pressure down and the gas fraction up together;
- without these limits an optimiser drifts toward deep, high-flow designs that a real pump cannot
  run (a lesson in 12.7). **Keep both limits on every ESP.**

Remedies when the limits bind: set the pump deeper, lower the flow per doublet and add a doublet,
choose a larger well diameter (less friction), keep a higher wellhead pressure, or specify a
gas-handling pump (with a sourced limit).

matches.text:
- **requirements of the case** (third-party limits: flow caps, brine cooling, reinjection, delivered
  energy): never loosened by the designer;
- **operating limits of equipment** (intake pressure, gas fraction, drive temperature): properties
  of the equipment chosen; change the equipment (and source its new limit) rather than delete the
  limit.

## 10.5 Sensitivity and uncertainty

Run them on the chosen design, sensitivity first, uncertainty only when the task asks: how, and how
many runs, in `knowledge/handbook-studies.md` section 3 (skill `economics`).

## 10.6 Staying out of infeasible regions

Most wasted searches come from ranges that include designs that cannot run. Before searching:

- Check the extremes by engineering: at the deepest depth and the highest flow, is the pump intake
  above its minimum and the gas fraction below its limit (4.3, 4.4)? At the shallowest depth, can
  the heat pump reach the supply with its lift (6.4)?
- Keep operating limits on every unit (4.4): without them the optimiser exploits unphysical
  designs.
- Prefer integer-plus-continuous searches with few leaves; fix what does not matter.
- When the search returns `feasible: false`, read the reason (11.7) and change ranges, options or
  the structure, not the requirement.

product. A demand derived from gas bills is fuel burnt, not heat delivered: ask which a file

| Kind of limit | Typical form | What it does to the costs |
|---|---|---|
| Number of doublets | a minimum and a maximum count | caps the geothermal capacity; each doublet adds drilling capex (§2.2) |
| Flow per doublet | a range in m3/h while running | sets pump size and pump electricity (§2.3, §3.3) |
| Brine cooling | a maximum temperature drop in K | caps the heat per doublet; the rest comes from a heat pump, a boiler or more wells |
| Running time of a doublet | a maximum share of the year | forces backup capacity for the days it stands still (boiler or electric boiler capex) |
| Equipment efficiency | a fixed pump efficiency | fixes the electricity per unit of flow and head |
| Mass balance | production equals injection | adds the injection pump and its electricity |
| Supply temperatures | a level per service | decides heat pump, boiler or deeper wells (§17.2) |
| Delivered energy | an unmet share of the yearly demand | sets how much backup the plant needs |
| Prescribed factors | a grid CO2 intensity, a price set by the client | moves CO2 and opex directly (§9.4) |

Read the limits before costing, and say in the report which of them drove the cost of the
chosen design.

matches.text:
- **Keep it in solution**: hold the surface loop above the bubble point (pressurised loop),
  inject the gas back with the brine. Simpler, no gas to handle, but needs pressure margin
  everywhere, and the gas never earns anything.
- **Separate it**: degas at a controlled pressure (5.2), then use or dispose of the gas (5.5). Needed
  when the gas content is high or the gas has value as fuel; it produces emissions that must be
  counted (5.6).

## 5.2 Degassers and separators

A degasser (gas separator) lets the free gas leave the liquid in a vessel at a set pressure. Its
design values are the vessel pressure (or pressure drop) and the separation efficiency. In gemini
the `Degasser` removes a share `separation_efficiency` of the free gas and applies a pressure loss;
dissolved gas that does not come out at the vessel pressure stays in the liquid (Henry's law and
residence time are not modelled) [gemini: `gemini/modules/treatment/degasser.py`].

Place the degasser upstream of the heat exchanger so that the exchanger sees liquid only, and after
the production wells are joined, so that one vessel serves all doublets. A lower vessel pressure
releases more gas but makes scaling more likely; a design without PVT data cannot predict the
dissolved share and must say so.

# 5 Brine chemistry and associated gas

This chapter covers what the brine carries besides heat: dissolved gas, salts, solids. Each can
stop a plant (scaling, gas-locked pumps, clogged injectors) or add emissions (methane, CO2).

## 5.1 Dissolved gas and why it comes out

Deep brines often carry dissolved gas, mainly CO2 and CH4 (and sometimes N2, H2S). The case
states it as a **gas-liquid ratio** (GLR, Nm3 of gas per m3 of liquid at standard conditions) and a
composition. A normal cubic metre is at 0 °C and 1.01325 bar(a) [standard: DIN 1343].

Gas stays dissolved while the pressure is above the bubble point. On the way up the pressure falls
and gas comes out: first in the well above the pump (two-phase flow, 4.2), then at the pump intake
if the intake pressure is low (4.4), then in surface equipment where the pressure is lowest.
Released CO2 raises the pH of the brine and drives carbonate scaling (5.3).

Two operating philosophies:
matches.section: 4 Wells and pumps > 4.8 Wells and pumps checklist

matches.name: knowledge/handbook-economics.md
matches.text:
Variable O&M scales with the energy produced: wear, consumables, part of the maintenance. DEA
version 0019 gives a plant variable O&M of 3.07 EUR/MWh of heat (EUR 2025) for its geothermal
sheets 45.1.b and 45.3 (catalogue row `opex-variable-dea-2025`, status *verified*; the row notes
that it includes chemical treatment). Do not add a separate chemical cost on top of a variable
O&M that already includes it.

### 3.3 Energy bought: electricity and gas

The largest running cost of a geothermal heat pump plant is usually electricity: ESPs, injection
pumps, circulation pumps, heat pumps and compression chillers. Gas is bought for peak boilers when
the produced gas does not suffice.

- Bill = energy bought in each step × price in that step, summed over the year.
- Price the energy at the **delivered price paid by the plant**: the consumption band, the network
  charges and the non-recoverable taxes that apply (chapter 10).
- For gas, state the heating value convention. Eurostat quotes gas prices per kWh of **gross**
  calorific value; a model that counts fuel on the **lower** heating value must convert, or the
  bill is off by the ratio of the two (about 10 % for natural gas; a general figure, check it for
  the gas in question). gemini prices gas per energy of its lower heating value (schema of
  `economics.energy.gas`).
- Co-produced gas burnt on site costs nothing to buy, but its combustion emits CO2 (chapter 9).

### 3.4 Chemicals and waste

- **Burn before you flare.** If a boiler or CHP needs heat anyway, the co-produced gas is free fuel.
  Size the boiler's base fuel use to the gas available, top up with grid gas, and send only the

matches.text:
### 2.1 Cost structure of a geothermal heating and cooling plant

The capex is the investment needed before the plant runs. For a deep geothermal heating and
cooling plant it splits into:

| Block | Items | Typical cost basis |
|---|---|---|
| Subsurface | Drilling, casing, completion, well testing, drill site | per m of well, per well, per site |
| Production lift | Electric submersible pump (ESP) or line-shaft pump | per kW of shaft power, per unit |
| Injection | Injection pump, filters | per kW, per unit |
| Gas handling | Degasser (separator), flare, gas make-up, CHP or boiler on the produced gas | fixed amount, per kW |
| Heat transfer | Brine-to-water heat exchangers | per W/K of conductance, per W of duty |
| Heat upgrade | Heat pumps, peak boilers, electric boilers | per W of capacity |
| Cold | Absorption, adsorption or compression chillers, coolers (dry or wet) | per W of capacity |
| Distribution inside the boundary | Pipes | per m, or per MW and m |
| Storage | Hot water or ice storage | per m3 or per MWh |
| Indirect | Engineering, permits, project management, owner's costs, contingency | % of direct cost |

In deep geothermal plants the wells usually dominate, followed by a heat pump where one raises
the temperature; read gemini's capex by module to see which (§16.2).

### 2.2 Drilling and wells: cost against depth

In a normally pressured aquifer the pore pressure is close to hydrostatic: p(z) ≈ ρ g z (gauge, with

depth without changing the reference pressure describes a different reservoir (QA-119).

## 3.2 Reservoir pressure at depth

In a normally pressured aquifer the pore pressure is close to hydrostatic: p(z) ≈ ρ g z (gauge, with
the water table at the surface). From a reference pressure p_ref at depth z_ref:

p(z) = p_ref + ρ g (z − z_ref)

[gemini: `gemini/physics/ground.py`, `reservoir_pressure`]. gemini applies it: the case gives the
pressure at `site.reservoir.reference_depth`, and a doublet designed at another depth gets the
pressure at its own depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `_doublets`]. Therefore **change the
plant's depth, not the case's reference depth**, to explore deeper wells: changing the reference
depth without changing the reference pressure describes a different reservoir (QA-119).

## 3.3 Productivity and injectivity

The productivity index (PI) relates the flow to the drawdown, Q = PI · (p_res − p_wf). For steady
radial Darcy flow into a well [textbook: Dake 1978]:

PI = 2π k h / ( μ · ( ln(r_e / r_w) + S ) )

with k the permeability, h the net thickness, μ the brine viscosity, r_e the drainage radius, r_w
the wellbore radius and S the skin. The injectivity index (II) has the same form for the injector.

# 3 The subsurface

## 3.1 Reservoir temperature from the gradient

In conductive settings the temperature rises roughly linearly with depth:

# 6. Alternatives considered

## 6.1 Why alternatives are reported

A single design proves only that it works, not that it is a good choice. Reporting the
alternatives shows the search was real and lets the reader see the price of each choice. For a
geothermal heating and cooling plant the usual alternatives differ in:

- how the supply temperature is reached (deeper wells, a heat pump, a boiler);
- how cold is made (absorption or adsorption chiller driven by geothermal heat, compression
  chiller, free cooling);
- how the associated gas is handled (flare, boiler, CHP);

## 3.2 Reservoir pressure at depth

In a normally pressured aquifer the pore pressure is close to hydrostatic: p(z) ≈ ρ g z (gauge, with
the water table at the surface). From a reference pressure p_ref at depth z_ref:

p(z) = p_ref + ρ g (z − z_ref)

[gemini: `gemini/physics/ground.py`, `reservoir_pressure`]. gemini applies it: the case gives the
pressure at `site.reservoir.reference_depth`, and a doublet designed at another depth gets the
pressure at its own depth [gemini: `gemini/engine/apply.py`, `_doublets`]. Therefore **change the
plant's depth, not the case's reference depth**, to explore deeper wells: changing the reference
depth without changing the reference pressure describes a different reservoir (QA-119).

## 3.3 Productivity and injectivity

The productivity index (PI) relates the flow to the drawdown, Q = PI · (p_res − p_wf). For steady
radial Darcy flow into a well [textbook: Dake 1978]:

PI = 2π k h / ( μ · ( ln(r_e / r_w) + S ) )

the wellbore radius and S the skin. The injectivity index (II) has the same form for the injector.

# 3 The subsurface

This chapter gives the reservoir values a design needs and how they follow from depth: temperature,
pressure, productivity, drawdown, thermal breakthrough. Most of them are properties of the site
(the case) and only the depth and well design are choices.

## 3.1 Reservoir temperature from the gradient

In conductive settings the temperature rises roughly linearly with depth:

T(z) = T_surface + G · z

with T_surface the mean surface (or reference) temperature and G the geothermal gradient. Typical
continental gradients are of the order of 25 to 35 K/km; sedimentary basins with thick insulating
cover can be higher [textbook: Stober and Bucher 2013]. The gradient of a site comes from the case
(measured wells, maps), never from a typical value.

In gemini the plant states only the depth; the case holds `site.ground.gradient` and
`site.ground.surface_temperature`, and the run derives the reservoir temperature at the plant's

output.skill:
[skill setting-the-case, sent with the first call of describe_case]
## The tools

### `accept_case`

Make the state's case the one the user gave, after the user approved its changes.

Only the design loop's driver holds this tool, after the user answered its question.

### `ask_economics`

Ask the user the ONE economics question from the rows you chose, and set what they approve.

Send only the exceptions: every economics key of the cost catalogue you do not name goes in
with its recommended row (sourced, verified, no upper bound or proxy, the latest year; a
real discount rate) and its other rows in `others`; a key with only placeholder rows is
open. Name a key to recommend another row (one of the site's country), to put it in `open`,
or with a value from a server or the user.
`values` holds each economics key with the row you recommend: `key` its path under
`economics` (`capex.heat_pump`, `energy.electricity`), `row` the catalogue row `id`
and, for a key whose rows differ, `others`, the ids of the rows you did not recommend
(`["drilling-nl-2013-2300m"]`). Send only ids: this tool reads each row's value, unit,
source, year, url and status from the knowledge base itself, so never copy them (copying
every row ran past the output limit). `value` with `source` (and `unit`, no `row`) is
for a value a knowledge document or a project file states (an assumptions document of the
case: `source` `knowledge/<name>` with its section), an MCP result or the user. `discount_rate` is a key too, in `values` or in
`open`. A value from a catalogue row is its `value_2015` in
`unit_2015`, EUR at 2015 prices, so this tool sets `currency` EUR and `price_year` 2015
itself: leave both out (without any row, name each in `values` or `open`). A row's unit
goes as the row writes it (`EUR/W electric`); a unit its key does not take is refused,
every one at once, before the user is asked. `open` names the keys no usable row gives, each
key once in `values` or `open`; `note` one line for the user. A field with
nothing to say is null or left out; a key whose value is null is open. The question's
options are approve all, change some and stop, and the user may type an answer instead. On
approve all, every value is set in the case's economics (`set_case`) with its row in
`about.sources`, and each becomes a confirmed assumption with its citation; the result says
what was set. On change some, ask which values change and to what, without options.

### `case_changes`

List how the state's case differs from the case the user or the project gave.

Each item has `path` (a section, `section.key`, `requirements.<name>` or `file <name>`),
`change` (`changed`, `removed` or `added`) and the `given` and `now` values. An
empty list means the case is the one the user gave. A design is verified only on that case:
any difference waits for the user's approval.

### `describe_case`

Say what each key of the case or its economics under `path` means, with its units.

`path` is a dotted key or a part of one, such as `site.air`, `demand.cooling`,
`requirements` (also what each option means) or `economics.capex`. Returns `keys`, one
line each: the key, its form and units, its meaning and where its value comes from.

### `list_profiles`

List the demand of the case: its heating and cooling services, with unit, window and peak.

### `read_case`

Return the case of the problem state, one of its sections, its economics or the schema.

`section` is a key of the case (`time`, `site`, `demand`, `utilities`,
`requirements`, `initial_state`), `economics` for the content of the economics file, or
`schema` for the JSON Schema of a case (and of the economics under `economics_schema`).
A section the case does not set yet returns `{section, unset: true, note}`.

### `read_profile`

Return the demand of a service (heating or cooling) of the case as a series in MW.

`start` and `end` are ISO 8601 times, both inclusive. `summary` gives the `peak` and
`minimum` with their time, the `mean` and the `energy` of the window, computed by
gemini's units: take a size from it, never from adding the series by hand.

### `save_profile`

Add a demand profile the user gave as values to the case's demand, and return the demand.

`values` are the demand of the `service` (heating or cooling), one per step in the power
unit `unit` (such as `MW`), from the ISO 8601 time `start` at a constant `step`, given
as `{"value": 1, "unit": "d"}`. gemini checks them (finite, not negative). They are written
to the run's case files as `data/<name>.csv` with a `time` column and the column `name`,
in `unit`, and the `power` of the service points at it; the rest of the demand is kept. A
profile that does not cover the case's `time` sets the time to the profile's own span and
step, in the same call. The service's temperatures and the other series must fit the result:
gemini rejects the case otherwise and nothing is stored.

### `set_case`

Set the case of the problem state: the project's case, changes to it, or both.

`source` is `project` to load the project's `case.json` (beside its data or among its
files, `list_files`) and the files it names, `origin` to go
back to the case the user or the project gave, or omitted to start from the state's case (an
empty one when it has none). `changes` is a JSON merge patch (RFC 7386) on the case: an
object merges into the case, a value replaces, null removes a key; it never holds
`requirements` or `economics` of a case that has them (on a new case, they and `files`
and `columns` in `changes` are taken as those arguments). `requirements` is
`{name: requirement or null}`: a requirement object adds or replaces the one of that name,
null removes it, and the others stay.
`economics` is a merge patch on the content of the case's economics file. `files` names
project files (`list_files`): their bytes go to gemini, under the same name, so a data file
is given to the case and never retyped: name it in `changes`, as the `file` of a series.
A project file the changes name is loaded even when `files` leaves it out. `columns`
renames header names of those files, such as `{"demand.csv": {"date": "time"}}`:
gemini reads a series' times from a column named `time`. Once a case is stored, send only
the keys that change: `changes` merges into it, and a rejected call stores nothing. The
sections are
in `read_case(section="schema")`, the exact schema. gemini validates the result: a rejected
case comes back with the path and message to fix, and nothing is stored; a case with values
missing is `case_incomplete`, every missing path in `suggestions`. The project's case, or
the first case of a chat, is the case the user gave; a design is verified only on it, so any
later change of it, economics included, waits for the user's approval. Write units as the
source gives them (gemini takes °C/km): a gas fraction in % is mol% (gemini converts
mol%), and a unit name as sources print it becomes gemini's name of it (`kg/m³` is
`kg/m3`, `mPa·s` is `mPa.s`, `MWth` is `MW`). With only the site's elevation, give
`site.air.pressure` as `{"elevation": {"value", "unit"}}`: set_case sets the ISA pressure
in Pa (ISO 2533:1975), never a value of yours. Returns the case, the state version
and `converted`, each value set_case mapped or converted (`{path, from, to, reason}`). It
comes after the one confirmation question, so a unit NAME it mapped, with `plants_need` paths
(by path and unit, no number), goes in the one follow-up `ask_user` after it; the ISA pressure
is never asked, the user confirms the elevation. Never use `calculate` for a case value.

Plus `missing` (only keys the case needs) and `disagreements`. Do not invent values: a value with no source is `missing`, never a typical value. ## The tools

### `list_files`

List the files of the project: `files`, each with `name`, `size` and `media_type`.

Read one with `read_rag`, and give a data file to the case with `set_case` `files`.

### `read_rag`

Read a project file, or a document of the knowledge base as `knowledge/<name>`, as text.

A long document with headings (a handbook of 25 to 50 pages with `#`, `##`, `###`) is read by
section, never page by page from the start:

- `read_rag(name, outline=true)`: the heading tree, each `{level, number, title, start, size}`
  (`number` is the title's own, such as `3.2`, else its place in the tree).
- `read_rag(name, section="3.2")` or `section="Pumps"` (a title, or a part of one): exactly that
  section with its subsections, paged with `start` inside it when it is longer than a page; the
  answer names the `section` read. An unknown section is refused with the headings it has.
- A knowledge hit of `search_rag` carries `section`, the heading path it falls in
  (`3 Wells > 3.2 Pumps`): read that whole section next with `section`.

CSV, TSV, JSON, Markdown and text files read as they are, and a PDF as its extracted text with
a `[page n]` marker before each page; another file is a `not_text` error. `start` is the
first character and `length` the number of characters, at most 20,000. Returns `name`,
`start`, `total`, `text` and `next`, where the following page starts (`null` at the
end). The first page of a CSV or TSV also has `table`: `columns`, the number of `rows`,
the `first_rows`, the `last_row` and the `span` its first column covers as a case's
time: `start`, `end` (exclusive, one step after the last row) and `step`, or `null`
when that column is not evenly spaced times. `columns` reads only those columns of a CSV or
TSV, in that order, such as the `id`, `path` and price of a cost table: a wide table costs
far fewer tokens so. `rows` (`{column: [text, ...]}`) reads only the rows whose value in
each named column starts with one of the texts, such as the paths of the keys a case lacks.
A CSV or TSV still longer than 20,000 characters after them gives no `text`: its `table`
outline and a `note`; find its rows with `search_rag` and read them by `rows`. A page
this run already read comes back as `already_read` with a `note` instead of its text: its
text is in the conversation, even with `force`, unless a compaction summarized it since;
after one, `force` reads it again until the whole document was read, then every page is
`already_read` with the references of the stored results. Nested runs share what the run
tree read.

### `search_rag`

## 3.1 Power and energy

A demand series gives **power** per step (`MW`). A daily file usually gives the mean power of
the day; a column in `MWh/d` is an energy, not a power, and is a unit to confirm. `MWth`,
`MWcool`, `MWc` are all `MW`: the suffix names the product. `MWe` is electricity, another
product. A demand derived from gas bills is fuel burnt, not heat delivered: ask which a file
holds.

## 3.2 The time axis and the time zone

- `time.start` and `time.end` without an offset are UTC; `end` is excluded
  (`gemini/gemini/case/time.py`).
- A **series** needs an offset (`2027-01-01T00:00:00Z`) on every timestamp, or a `time_zone`
  (an IANA name such as `Europe/Amsterdam`) for the file. Without both, gemini refuses the
  series: there is no default zone (`gemini/gemini/units/inputs.py`, `from_series`).
- With a `time_zone` and a step of one day or more, gemini matches the rows to the case's steps
  by local calendar date, so a 23- or 25-hour day of daylight saving does no harm.
- A zone that no file and no user message states is an assumption: propose it in the one
  question with its reason (the site's location), `source: agent`, never "the user chose it".
- The time column is read as `time`; a column of another name (`date`) is named in `columns`
  when the file is given (skill `setting-the-case`).
- A year has 365 or 366 daily rows; check against the calendar.
- The economic analysis period (often decades) is an economics value, not `time`.

## 3.3 Checks on a demand series

Report each failure as a flaw (§1.4); correct none.

| Check | Fails when |
|---|---|
| count | rows differ from the span over the step |
| gaps, duplicates | a missing or repeated time |
| sign, finite | a negative or non-finite value (gemini refuses them) |
| unit | the peak or total is far from the brief's values for checking (§1.3) |
| season | heating peaks in summer or cooling in winter (northern hemisphere) |
| span | the case's span differs from the file's: the span is wrong, never the data |
| zero days | many zero days of cooling are normal; note how many (they matter for `when`, §6.6) |
| base load | a heating series that never reaches zero has a summer base: say so |

## 3.4 Resolution

| Step | Shows | Hides |
|---|---|---|
| hourly | daily pattern, true peak, storage cycles | nothing relevant for sizing |
| daily | season, cold spells, days a source runs | the hourly peak, which is higher than the daily mean |
| monthly | season only | peaks, cold spells, zero days |

A daily case sizes on daily means: name the hidden hourly peak as a limitation. Never build a
finer series from a coarser one, nor a series from a peak and an annual energy: ask for a
series file, the values, or a constant power.

List the files of the project: `files`, each with `name`, `size` and `media_type`.

### `read_rag`

Read a project file, or a document of the knowledge base as `knowledge/<name>`, as text.

A long document with headings (a handbook of 25 to 50 pages with `#`, `##`, `###`) is read by
section, never page by page from the start:

- `read_rag(name, outline=true)`: the heading tree, each `{level, number, title, start, size}`
  (`number` is the title's own, such as `3.2`, else its place in the tree).

  section with its subsections, paged with `start` inside it when it is longer than a page; the
  answer names the `section` read. An unknown section is refused with the headings it has.

  (`3 Wells > 3.2 Pumps`): read that whole section next with `section`.

CSV, TSV, JSON, Markdown and text files read as they are, and a PDF as its extracted text with
a `[page n]` marker before each page; another file is a `not_text` error. `start` is the
first character and `length` the number of characters, at most 20,000. Returns `name`,

time: `start`, `end` (exclusive, one step after the last row) and `step`, or `null`
when that column is not evenly spaced times. `columns` reads only those columns of a CSV or
TSV, in that order, such as the `id`, `path` and price of a cost table: a wide table costs
far fewer tokens so. `rows` (`{column: [text, ...]}`) reads only the rows whose value in
each named column starts with one of the texts, such as the paths of the keys a case lacks.
A CSV or TSV still longer than 20,000 characters after them gives no `text`: its `table`
outline and a `note`; find its rows with `search_rag` and read them by `rows`. A page
this run already read comes back as `already_read` with a `note` instead of its text: its
text is in the conversation, even with `force`, unless a compaction summarized it since;
after one, `force` reads it again until the whole document was read, then every page is
`already_read` with the references of the stored results. Nested runs share what the run
tree read.

Search the project's documents and files and the knowledge base; return `{matches, note}`.
